questions_and_answers.question_text: How is the verb gěi used in No. 3?
Where do prepositional verbs and their objects come in a Chinese sentence?
How does this differ from English word order?
What is the effect of reduplicating huàn?
Write the Chinese for "Please change it for me."
What does gěi mean when used prepositionally?
Write the Chinese for "Please write your address for me."

answers.answer_text: Qǐng ni gěi wo xiě nǐde dìzhǐ.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "He bought an electric fan for his younger sister."

answers.answer_text: Tā gěi mèimei mǎile yíge diànshàn.

questions_and_answers.question_text: In Chinese, does gěi wo come before or after the main verb?

answers.answer_text: Before the main verb — whereas English "for me" follows the verb.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Why is the reduplicated form huànhuan used rather than plain huàn?

answers.answer_text: Because reduplication makes the request milder and more polite.

articles.text:
3. B: Qǐng ni gěi wo huànhuan.       Please change it for me.

Notes on No. 3

Gěi wo: In No. 3 the verb gěi is used prepositionally to mean "for." Prepositional verbs and their objects come before the main verb in a sentence. Notice that while gěi wo precedes the main verb in Chinese, "for me" follows the verb in English.

PREPOSITIONAL VERB  |  ITS OBJECT  |  MAIN VERB
gěi                 |  wo          |  huànhuan

Qǐng ni gěi wo kànkan nǐde        Please let me look at that book
nèiběn shū.                       of yours.
Tā gěi mèimei mǎile yíge          He bought an electric fan for
diànshàn.                         his younger sister.
Qǐng ni gěi wo xiě nǐde           Please write your address for me.
dìzhǐ.

Huànhuan: The reduplication of huàn in No. 3 makes the request milder and more polite.
